The initial energy content of the leathery-shelled egg of the Flatback turtle (Natator depressus) has been quantified through analysis of yolk composition, yielding an average value of 323,000 joules  based on nine eggs collected from Eighty Mile Beach. Hatchlings emerge after a total incubation duration of approximately 57 days [ab = approximately 57 days] at a constant incubation temperature of 29.85 °C [T = 29.85 °C], a figure that accounts for the 51.23 days required for embryonic development within the shell plus an additional six days needed for nest emergence and yolk-sac absorption. The average straight carapace length (SCL) at hatching, derived from the same cohort of thirteen hatchlings, was measured at 5.461 centimeters . This remarkably consistent size at emergence is largely determined by the fixed volume of the yolk-laden egg, which constrains the maximum dimensions of the pre-emergent lecithotrophic larva. In the coastal waters of Western Australia, tagged nesting females have been recorded reaching a maximum curved carapace length (CCL) of 98.5 centimeters [Li = 98.5 centimeters] at Port Hedland, representing the upper size limit for this species in that region.

The onset of reproductive maturity appears to be linked to a threshold body size in this species, with the minimum curved carapace length among nesting females recorded at Cemetery Beach measuring 82.7 centimeters [Lp = 82.7 centimeters]. This morphological milestone signals that an individual has successfully navigated the juvenile and sub-adult phases of growth and entered the reproductively viable stage of life. Primiparous females at Mon Repos in Queensland are estimated to begin their first reproduction event at approximately 6,935 days after hatching [tR = approximately 6,935 days after hatching], a calculation derived from 19 years of age at first nesting less the two years during which reproductive allocation is believed to commence prior to the first observed clutch; this timing aligns with data from tagged flatbacks in Western Australia conducted under mean annual water temperatures of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. Prior to this first breeding event, individuals pass through a prolonged juvenile phase characterized by steady somatic growth. The wet body mass at puberty, which corresponds to the weight at which gonadal activation first becomes possible, has been estimated at approximately 60,000 grams [Wwp = approximately 60,000 grams], a substantial fraction of the ultimate adult body mass.

For a long-lived marine chelonian, the maximum lifespan represents a critical demographic parameter integral to population viability analysis. At Mon Repos, combining an estimated 21 years to reach first breeding with a subsequent 30-year nesting window and an additional 20-year period of post-reproductive survival yields a maximum projected lifespan of approximately 25,915 days [am = approximately 25,915 days] for females, a figure consistent with longevity records from other sea turtle species within t at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]he Cheloniidae. This exceptionally long life, spent under sea surface temperatures averaging 26 °C [T = 26 °C], allows for the accumulation of many reproductive events over the course of an individual's life. The reproductive output of a mature female is substantial; females at three Western Australian rookeries lay an average of 46.6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 46.6 eggs per clutch] and produce roughly 2.84 nests per nesting season [F_R_i = roughly 2.84 nests per nesting season] at 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. With an average interval of 1.6 years between successive nesting seasons, this translates to a sustained high fecundity across decades of adult life.

A detailed analysis of the yolk mass and wet weight of freshly oviposited eggs provides further insight into the maternal investment strategy of Natator depressus. Individual fertilised ova, still enclosed in their pliable, parchment-like shells, weigh an average of 66.54 grams [Ww0 = 66.54 grams] at deposition. This substantial investment of maternal resources is reflected in the measured wet mass of the hatchling at the moment of nest emergence, which is approximately 45.42 grams . The difference between the initial egg mass and the hatchling mass largely represents the energetic substrate consumed during the 51.23 days  required for full embryonic development and the subsequent six-day yolk-sac absorption period, both occurring at the stable incubation temperature of 29.85 °C [T = 29.85 °C]. The progressive absorption of yolk nutrients sustains the embryo throughout the incubation period and partially supports the hatchling for a brief period of endotrophic life. It is noteworthy that the straight carapace length at birth and at hatching are virtually identical (5.461 centimeters) [Lb = 5.461 centimeters], as the animal does not grow in carapace length during the few days it spends inside the nest chamber following eclosion.

Sexual maturation in the Flatback turtle is a gradual process, and the acquisition of the full adult body mass is not a prerequisite for the onset of breeding; rather, a threshold somatic size appears to trigger the reproductive endocrine cascade. The maximum wet body mass attained by adult females in this species has been documented at 94,800 grams [Wwi = 94,800 grams], representing the upper extreme of asymptotic body mass for the species. This ultimate size is considerably larger than the body mass at maturity of approximately 60,000 grams [Wwp = approximately 60,000 grams], indicating that females continue to grow substantially after initiating their reproductive careers. This pattern of continued post-maturity growth is common among long-lived reptiles with indeterminate growth potential. The extended lifespan of approximately 25,915 days [am = approximately 25,915 days] provides a long window for this gradual accretion o at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]f body tissues. When comparing the CCL at puberty of 82.7 centimeters with the ultimate CCL of 98.5 centimeters, it is clear that significant somatic expansion occurs well after the age at first reproduction, likely as a result of continued resource acquisition and allocation to structural growth in intervals between successive nesting seasons.
